query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of boron (≈0.1 at.%) to a refractory high‐entropy alloy (such as HfMoNbTaTiZr) will promote the intergranular precipitation of fine (Hf, Zr)B2 borides that enhance grain-boundary cohesion. This microstructural modification is hypothesized to improve ductility and uniform deformability (i.e. higher fracture strain and work-hardening ability) under both quasi‐static and dynamic (impact) loading without sacrificing the alloy’s high strength or its capacity for impact-induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., HfMoNbTaTiZr) with a primarily single-phase BCC solid-solution structure that exhibits limited ductility due to grain-boundary brittleness.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of a minor boron addition during alloy synthesis/melting.
generation.conditions: Tests carried out at room temperature under quasi-static and high-strain-rate (impact) loading conditions typical for energetic structural materials; the alloy should have a BCC matrix amenable to minor intergranular phase formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The nucleation and growth of fine, intergranular (Hf, Zr)B2 borides at grain boundaries, which reinforce the boundaries without altering the matrix significantly.
generation.mechanism: Boron atoms segregate at the grain boundaries during alloy solidification, precipitating as borides that increase grain boundary cohesion. This limits premature intergranular fracture and promotes a more uniform deformation. Because the bulk BCC matrix remains largely unaltered, the high strength and the impact-induced energy release characteristics (a key feature for energetic structural materials) are maintained.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the boron-doped alloy should exhibit a significant increase in fracture strain and work-hardening rate (indicating improved ductility and uniform deformability) while retaining similar yield and ultimate strengths and preserving the dynamic energy-release behavior under impact.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy, which typically shows limited ductility due to intergranular fracture and suboptimal work hardenability, even though it presents high strength and potential for energetic performance.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected for similar BCC-based refractory HEAs where minor boron additions lead to controlled intergranular boride precipitation. The hypothesis may not hold if boron leads to excessive or coarse secondary phase formation or in systems where other alloying elements dominate the intergranular behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While the positive effect of boron on ductility via grain-boundary strengthening is supported by studies on similar systems, the precise quantitative balance between ductility improvement and retention of energetic properties under dynamic loading conditions remains to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same base refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., HfMoNbTaTiZr): one set with a 0.1 at.% boron addition and one untreated control. Subject both sets to comprehensive mechanical testing including quasi-static compression/tensile tests and high-strain-rate (impact) testing. Use high-speed imaging and appropriate sensors to capture any impact-induced energy release behaviors. Complement the mechanical tests with detailed microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM, EDS) to confirm the presence and distribution of nanoscale boride precipitates at the grain boundaries.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate strength (under static and dynamic loading)
Dynamic response parameters (reaction delay time, energy release rate) during impact tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in ductility (e.g., higher fracture strain and work-hardening rate) without a measurable decrease in yield strength or dynamic energy release performance compared to the untreated control, then the hypothesis should be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was developed in this study, and the addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%, RHEA-B) further overcame the grain-boundary brittleness. As indicated by the microstructural observations and chemical analyses, a simple BCC-phase, solid-solution structure was formed in the matrices of both the alloys. The addition of boron did not obviously increase the hardness of the matrix but induced the intergranular precipitation of the HCP-phase (Hf, Zr)B2 borides which markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Attributable to the lattice distortions caused by the random distribution of different constituent elements, a diminished anisotropy in the mechanical properties was noticed, and the deformation behavior was mediated by many small slips on multiple {110} planes. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion with the addition of boron and the intergranular precipitation of borides, the work hardenability and ductility of the alloy were effectively improved, and the failure mode obviously changed from a mainly intergranular facture to a major portion of the transgranular fracture.
